mn28:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.
mn28:1.3: There the venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus thus:
mn28:2.1: ‘Friends, just as the footprint of any living being that walks can be placed within an elephant’s footprint, and so the elephant’s footprint is declared the chief of them because of its great size,
mn28:2.2: so too, whatever profitable dhammas there are can all be included in the Four Noble Truths.
mn28:2.4: In the Noble Truth of Suffering, in the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, in the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and in the Noble Truth of the Way leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
mn28:3.1: ‘And what is the Noble Truth of Suffering?
mn28:3.2: Birth is suffering, ageing is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair are suffering; not to get what one wants is suffering; in short the five aggregates affected by clinging are suffering.
mn28:3.3: ‘And what are the five aggregates affected by clinging?
mn28:3.4: They are: the form aggregate affected by clinging, the feeling aggregate affected by clinging, the perception aggregate affected by clinging, the formations aggregate affected by clinging, the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging.
mn28:4.1: ‘And what is the form aggregate affected by clinging?
mn28:4.2: It is the four great primary elements and any form derived from them.
mn28:5.1: ‘And what are the four great primary elements?
mn28:5.2: They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element and the air element.
mn28:6.2: The earth element can be either in oneself or external.
mn28:6.3: ‘What is the earth element in oneself?
mn28:6.4: Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified and clung-to, that is to say,
mn28:6.5: head-hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lights, bowels, entrails, gorge, dung, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, that is solid, solidified and clung-to:
mn28:6.6: this is called earth element in oneself.
mn28:6.7: ‘Now earth element in oneself and external earth element are simply earth element.
mn28:6.8: And that should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.”
mn28:6.9: When a man sees it with right understanding as it actually is thus, he becomes dispassionate towards the earth element, and he fades lust for the earth element out of his mind.
mn28:7.1: ‘Now there is the occasion when the external earth element is disturbed
mn28:7.2: and then the external earth element vanishes.
mn28:7.3: ‘For even this external earth element, great as it is, is describable as impermanent, as subject to destruction, as subject to disappearance, as subject to change,
mn28:7.4: so what of this body, which is clung to by craving and lasts but a while? There can be no (considering) that as “I” or “mine” or “am”.
mn28:8.1: ‘So then, (having seen this element as it actually is, thus,) if others abuse and scold, curse and threaten a bhikkhu, he understands thus:
mn28:8.2: “This painful feeling born of ear contact has arisen in me.
mn28:8.6: Then he sees that contact is impermanent, that feeling is impermanent, that perception is impermanent, that formations are impermanent, and that consciousness is impermanent.
mn28:8.7: And his mind, which has already made an element (constituent of the form aggregate) its objective support, enters into that (new objective support now contemplated) and acquires confidence, steadiness and decision.
mn28:9.1: ‘Now if others attack that bhikkhu with unwished-for, undesired and disagreeable
mn28:9.2: contact of fists, clods, sticks or knives,
mn28:9.4: “This body is a thing such that contact with fists, clods, sticks and knives takes place in it.
mn28:9.5: But this has been said by the Blessed One in his discourse on the Simile of the Saw:
mn28:9.6: “Even if bandits savagely severed limb from limb with a two-handled saw, he who entertained hate in his heart on that account would not be one who carried out my teaching.”
mn28:9.7: So tireless energy shall be aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness established, my body shall be tranquil and unexcited, my mind shall be concentrated and unified.
mn28:9.8: And now let contact with fists, clods, sticks and knives take place in this body; for this is just how the Buddha’s message is put into effect.’
mn28:10.1: ‘If, when he thus recollects the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, equanimity does not persist in him with the profitable as its support,
mn28:10.2: then he arouses a sense of urgency thus:
mn28:10.3: “It is loss for me, it is no gain for me, it is bad for me, it is no good for me,
mn28:10.4: that when I recollect the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha thus, equanimity does not persist in me with the profitable as its support.”
mn28:10.5: Just as when a daughter-in-law sees her father-in-law, she has a sense of urgency,
mn28:10.8: ‘But if when a bhikkhu recollects the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha thus, equanimity becomes established in him with what is profitable as its support, then he is satisfied.
mn28:10.9: And at that point, friends, much has been done by the bhikkhus.
mn28:11.2: The water element can be either in oneself or external.
mn28:11.3: ‘What is the water element in oneself?
mn28:11.4: ‘Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung-to, that is to say,
mn28:11.5: bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil-of-the-joints, urine, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung-to:
mn28:11.6: this is called water element in oneself.
mn28:11.7: ‘Now water element in oneself and external water element are simply water element.
mn28:11.8: That should be seen with right understanding as it actually is thus: “This is not mine, this not I, this is not my self.”
mn28:11.9: When a man sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, he becomes dispassionate towards the water element, he fades lust for the water element out of his mind.
mn28:12.1: ‘Now there is an occasion when the water element is disturbed.
mn28:12.2: It carries away village, town, city, district and country.
mn28:12.3: There is an occasion when the waters in the great ocean sink down a hundred leagues, two hundred leagues … seven hundred leagues.
mn28:12.4: There is an occasion when the water in the great ocean stands seven palm trees deep, six palm trees deep … two palm trees deep, only a palm tree deep.
mn28:12.5: There is an occasion when the waters in the great ocean stand seven fathoms deep, six … only a fathom deep.
mn28:12.6: There is an occasion when the waters in the great ocean stand half fathom deep, only waist deep, only knee deep, only ankle deep.
mn28:12.7: There is an occasion when the waters in the great ocean are not enough to wet even the joint of a finger.
mn28:12.8: ‘For even this external water element, great as it is, is describable as impermanent, as subject to destruction, as subject to disappearance, as subject to change,
mn28:13.1: so what of this body which is clung to by craving and lasts but a while? There can be no (considering) that as “I” or “mine” or “am”.
mn28:14.1: ‘So then, (having seen this element as it actually is, thus), if others abuse … (repeat paras. 11-14) …
mn28:15.1: much has been done by that bhikkhu.
mn28:16.2: The fire element can either be in oneself or external.
mn28:16.3: ‘And what is the fire element in oneself?
mn28:16.4: ‘Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, and clung-to, that is to say,
mn28:16.5: that whereby one is warmed, ages, and is consumed, and that whereby what is eaten, drunk, chewed and tasted gets completely digested, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, and clung-to:
mn28:16.6: this is called fire element in oneself.
mn28:16.7: ‘Now fire element in oneself and external fire element are simply fire element.
mn28:16.8: That should be seen with right understanding as it actually is thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.”
mn28:16.9: When a man sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, he becomes dispassionate towards the fire element, he fades lust for the fire element out of his mind.
mn28:17.1: ‘There is an occasion when the external fire element is disturbed.
mn28:17.2: It burns up village, town, city, district and country.
mn28:17.3: It only goes out when it comes to green grass, or to a road, or to a rock, or to water or a fair open space, for want of fuel.
mn28:17.4: There is an occasion when they seek to make a fire even with fowls’ claws and hide-parings.
mn28:17.5: ‘For even this external fire element, great as it is, is describable as impermanent, as subject to destruction, as subject to disappearance, as subject to change,
mn28:17.6: so what of this body, which is clung-to by craving and lasts but a while? There can be no (considering) that as “I” or “mine” or “am”.’
mn28:18-20.1: ‘So then, (having seen this element as it actually is, thus) if others abuse (repeat paras. 11-14) …
mn28:18-20.2: much has been done by that bhikkhu.
mn28:21.2: The air element can either be in oneself or external.
mn28:21.3: ‘What is the air element in oneself?
mn28:21.4: ‘Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung-to, that is to say,
mn28:21.5: up-going winds (forces), down-going winds (forces), winds (forces) in the belly, winds (forces) in the bowels, winds (forces) that pervade all the limbs, in-breath and out-breath, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung-to:
mn28:21.6: this is called air element in oneself.
mn28:21.7: ‘Now air element in oneself and external air element are simply air element.
mn28:21.8: And that should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not myself.”
mn28:21.9: When a man sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, he becomes dispassionate towards the air element, he fades lust for the air element out of his mind.
mn28:22.1: ‘There is an occasion when the external air element is disturbed.
mn28:22.2: It sweeps away village, town, city, district and country.
mn28:22.3: There is an occasion in the last month of the hot season when they seek wind by means of a fan or bellows and even the strands of straw in the drip-fringe of the thatch do not stir.
mn28:22.4: ‘For even this external air element, great as it is, is describable as impermanent, as subject to destruction, as subject to disappearance, as subject to change,
mn28:22.5: so what of this body, which is clung-to and lasts but a while? There can be no (considering) that as “I” or “mine” or “am”.

mn28:25.1: ‘If, when he thus recollects the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, equanimity does not persist in him with the profitable as its support,
mn28:25.2: then he arouses a sense of urgency thus:
mn28:25.3: “It is loss for me, it is no gain for me, it is bad for me, it is no good for me,
mn28:25.4: that when I recollect the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha thus, equanimity does not persist in me with the profitable as its support.”
mn28:25.5: Just as when a daughter-in-law sees her father-in-law, she has a sense of urgency,
mn28:25.6: so too, if a bhikkhu recollects the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha thus, and equanimity does not persist in him with the profitable as its support,
mn28:25.7: he arouses a sense of urgency thus:
mn28:25.8: “It is loss for me, it is no gain for me, it is bad for me, it is no good for me,
mn28:25.9: that when I recollect the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha thus, equanimity does not persist in me with the profitable as its support.”
mn28:25.10: ‘But if when a bhikkhu recollects the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha thus, equanimity becomes established in him with what is profitable as its support, then he is satisfied.
mn28:25.11: And at that point, friends, much has been done by the bhikkhu.
mn28:26.1: ‘Just as when a space is enclosed by timber and creepers, grass and clay, there comes to be the term “house”,
mn28:26.2: so too, when a space is enclosed by bones and sinews, flesh and skin, there comes to be the term “form”.
mn28:27.1: ‘If the eye in oneself were intact but no external forms came to its threshold (of consciousness) and there were no appropriate (conscious) engagement, then there would be no manifestation of the appropriate class of consciousness.
mn28:27.2: If the eye in oneself were intact and external forms came to its threshold but there were no appropriate (conscious) engagement, there would be no manifestation of the appropriate class of consciousness.
mn28:27.3: But it is owing to the fact that the eye in oneself is intact and that external forms come to its threshold, and that there is the appropriate (conscious) engagement, that there is manifestation of the appropriate class of consciousness.
mn28:28.1: ‘Whatever form of what has come to be thus, is included in the form aggregate affected by clinging. Whatever feeling of what has come to be thus, is included in the feeling aggregate affected by clinging. Whatever perception of what has come to be thus, is included in the perception aggregate affected by clinging. Whatever formations of what has come to be thus, are included in the formations aggregate affected by clinging. Whatever consciousness of what has come to be thus, is included in the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging.
mn28:28.3: “This, it seems, is how there comes to be inclusion, gathering, amassing into these five aggregates affected by clinging.
mn28:28.4: Now this has been said by the Blessed One:
mn28:28.5: “He who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma:
mn28:28.6: he who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination.”
mn28:28.7: And these five aggregates affected by clinging are dependently arisen.
mn28:28.8: The wish for reliance on, approval or acceptance of, these five aggregates affected by clinging is the origin of suffering.
mn28:28.9: The removal of wishing and lust, the abandoning of wishing and lust for them is the cessation of suffering.”
mn28:28.10: And at this point too, friends, much has been done by the bhikkhu.
mn28:29-30.1: ‘If the ear in oneself were intact but no external sounds came to its threshold …
mn28:31-32.1: If the nose in oneself were intact but no external smells came to its threshold …
mn28:33-34.1: If the tongue in oneself were intact but no external flavours came to its threshold …
mn28:35-36.1: If the body in oneself were intact but no external tangibles came to its threshold …
mn28:37.1: ‘If the mind in oneself were intact but no external dhammas came to its threshold … and there were no appropriate (conscious) engagement, then there would be no manifestation of the appropriate class of consciousness.

mn28:38.2: But it is owing to the fact that the mind in oneself is intact and that external dhammas come to its threshold, and that there is the appropriate (conscious) engagement, that there is manifestation of the appropriate class of consciousness.

mn28:38.6: Now this has been said by the Blessed One:
mn28:38.7: “He who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma:
mn28:38.8: he who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination.”
mn28:38.9: And these five aggregates affected by clinging are dependently arisen.
mn28:38.10: The wish for reliance on, approval or acceptance of, these five aggregates affected by clinging is the origin of suffering.
mn28:38.11: The removal of wishing and lust, the abandoning of wishing and lust for them is the cessation of suffering.”
mn28:38.12: And at this point too, friends, much has been done by the bhikkhu.’
mn28:38.13: That is what the venerable Sāriputta said.
mn28:38.14: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in his words.
